newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Kikkoman looks West but also eyes China.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Kikkoman looks West but also eyes China.

text.p: As Japanese consumers munch on more hamburgers and choose french fries over fried noodles, the world's leading soy sauce maker is looking to the West as the future for oriental flavourings.

With limited scope to boost sales in the saturated home market, Kikkoman Corp says it is looking to the United States and Europe for new profit opportunities but is also eyeing China as a potentially promising market closer to home.

Kikkoman president Yuzaburo Mogi, speaking in an interview with Reuters, said the firm was focusing on overseas markets where soy sauce consumption is on the rise, as well as new soy-sauce based products to offset the tight home market.

With a second plant in California due to go into operation next year and a new factory being built in the Netherlands to provide a European base, Kikkoman is aiming to expand its overseas presence by marketing Japan's most famous brand of soy sauce as a multi-purpose, international seasoning.
"We feel that soy sauce is a kind of all-purpose seasoning," said Mogi in the interview late on Monday.

"If we have too much of a Japanese or Asian image, they (consumers) will only use soy sauce for Chinese food. We would like to let customers use soy sauce not only for Chinese food but also for local dishes."

While Japan's fondness for foreign food and cheaper varieties of standard soy sauce have capped domestic growth, more and more Westerners are tucking into Asian food in restaurants and splashing soy sauce into their woks at home.

The West is also seen as a growth market for soy-sauce spinoffs, like blended steak sauces and marinades, and other new products which Kikkoman hopes will put its profits back on a healthy rising curve after a couple of lean years. In the lucrative American market, its biggest rival is La Choy.

In the year to end-December 1996, Kikkoman made a group net profit of 7.29 billion yen ($62.8 million), compared with 4.45 billion yen ($38.3 million) a year earlier, on slightly increased sales of 206 billion yen ($1.77 billion), although earnings fell at the operating level. The company's latest forecast for 1997 is for a group net profit of 6.60 billion yen ($56.8 million).

Despite the Western focus, Mogi also said Kikkoman was on the lookout for opportunities in Asia, and may take on Chinese makers on their home turf in the years to come if the country looks like being a rich new revenue source.

"I think the next possibility...is China," he said. "In China we don't have a large existing market...but if we start marketing in China I think we can increase sales to a certain extent to justify having a plant there."
Kikkoman already has a plant in Singapore and a factory in Taiwan to cater to the Asian market.

Despite the potential size of the Chinese market, the company is taking a cautious approach to selling Japanese-brand soy sauce in the land which developed the art of soy sauce production centuries ago.

"The problem is that Chinese soy sauce is cheap, so if our price is too high it's a problem," said Mogi. "So far we haven't done anything but fortunately the income of Chinese people is increasing year by year so I think within several years we might be able to market (our products) and also build a factory there."

Analysts said the international outlook is positive as there is plenty of room for growth in overseas markets, particularly Europe, although it would take time to feel the financial benefit of any move into China.
Kikkoman, the world's best-selling brand of soy sauce, would be marketed as a premium soy sauce for the discerning Chinese consumer, Mogi said.
Kikkoman has sounded out Chinese authorities on an informal basis but had not yet gone into detail about the possible scale of any move into China, he said.
"We haven't decided yet but I think some sort of joint venture would be a good idea," he said.
"I think maybe we would start with a very small investment," he said, without giving any specific estimates. "But sometimes, you know, a small child becomes a strong and healthy adult." ($1=116 yen)
